3.2 Effects of figure characteristics

Removing censoring marks affected KM curve accuracy and agreement in event counts differently.

For native PDFs, TAAE barely changed (difference, -5.9 × 10 -6 ; 95% CI, -1.7 × 10 -5 to 6.7 × 10 -6 ), but reconstructed event totals matched the original records in both groups in only 28 of 32 datasets without marks, compared with all 32 when marks were present. Cox log-HR errors also increased for native PDFs (S1 Text). For PNG300 images, removing marks increased mean TAAE by 0.0227 (95% CI, 0.0046 to 0.0410; Fig 4).

The post hoc analysis showed that small KM curve errors did not guarantee accurate event counts, even when both were evaluated after month 24. For native PDFs without censoring marks, event counts were correct through month 24 in all 32 datasets, but four datasets had one extra event after month 24. All four errors occurred within the later follow-up period evaluated, yet mean curve errors remained very small with and without marks (1.41 × 10 -5 and 1.12 × 10 -5 pp, respectively; S12 Table in S1 Text).

Lower image resolution and JPEG compression both increased KM reconstruction error. Compared with PNG300, reducing resolution to 150 dpi increased mean TAAE by 0.0295 (95% CI, 0.0110 to 0.0489), while reducing it to 100 dpi increased TAAE by 0.1305 (95% CI, 0.1100 to 0.1528).

Converting PNG100 to quality-75 JPEG further increased mean TAAE by 0.0648 (95% CI, 0.0275 to 0.1005; Fig 4).

Saving a PNG image as a PDF did not restore the high reconstruction accuracy of native vector PDFs. Across the same 32 datasets, mean TAAE was 0.104 pp for image-only PDFs, compared with 3.40 × 10 -5 for native vector PDFs and 0.0891 for PNG300 images. The mean paired difference between image-only PDFs and PNG300 was 0.0154 (95% CI, -0.0017 to 0.0321; S1 Text; S2 Figure ).

These findings support the interpretation that readable vector information contributes to the reconstruction advantage of native PDFs, beyond the PDF file format itself.

Native PDFs remained more accurate than PNG300 images when the KM figures were redrawn using survminer. Across all 16 datasets, native PDFs had lower TAAE, with mean errors of 0.000926 pp compared with 0.141 pp for PNG300. 3.3 Exploratory comparison with an automated digitization-Guyot workflow 4 Discussion

Preserving vector information improved KM reconstruction in this paired simulation study using a single tool-enabled language model. Native PDFs yielded lower curve errors than matched PNG300 inputs in every completed pair. However, the average PNG errors in RMST contrasts and Cox log-hazard ratios were small. The study establishes a difference in numerical fidelity within the evaluated workflow, without establishing clinically consequential changes in treatment comparisons or meta-analytic conclusions.

The saved programs provide a plausible explanation for the format difference: native-PDF reconstructions extracted stored curve paths, whereas PNG reconstructions estimated coordinates from pixels. An unchanged PNG embedded in a PDF did not recover the accuracy of the vector source.

Earlier work demonstrated direct coordinate extraction from vector scientific figures, and RESOLVE-IPD applies related ideas to survival reconstruction [17, 30]. Our paired experiment quantifies the combined effect of information preservation and the agent's response to that information. It does not establish that an LLM is necessary for accurate vector reconstruction. Nor should its performance be assumed to apply to a chat interface that cannot inspect vector objects or execute code.

Our findings complement the clinical validation by Everest et al., who found that RMST reconstruction accuracy was generally not associated with figure type across different published trials [18]. Their comparison and ours differ in design and outcome, and the small RMST discrepancies observed here do not establish a substantive contradiction. Assessing practical importance requires attention to the intended estimand, its uncertainty, and the distribution of errors rather than the frequency with which one format has the smaller error.

Accurate KM curves do not necessarily imply accurate recovery of individual event records.

In the post hoc analysis, all four native-PDF event-count discrepancies occurred after month 24, outside the primary curve-error evaluation window. However, KM curve errors remained very small when evaluated over the same supported later follow-up, indicating that the discrepancy could not be explained by different evaluation windows alone. These findings support checking event totals and numbers at risk alongside KM curve agreement when validating reconstructed records.

The conventional comparison also requires qualification. The Guyot analyses showed that closer KM curve agreement did not always lead to more accurate treatment estimates. Although exact coordinates reduced curve error, mean RMST-contrast and Cox log-HR errors increased.

Dataset-level diagnostics suggested that these differences reflected reduced cancellation between arm-specific RMST errors and changes in late event and censoring allocations. For some arms, coordinate substitution also changed the final risk-table interval constraints ( S8 Table in S1 Text).

These results describe how the Guyot workflow responds to different inputs rather than separate contributions of digitization and reconstruction error. The LLM-Guyot comparison likewise reflects differences between the two implemented workflows, including their use of censoring marks and opportunities for revision. Future comparisons should use validated implementations and explicitly matched information where the aim is to isolate algorithmic performance.

For practice, researchers should preserve original vector figures when available and verify that their extraction workflow can use the encoded information. Saving a screenshot as a PDF does not restore vector coordinates. Journals and repositories can support reuse by retaining vector graphics and reporting risk counts and censoring information [31, 32]. This recommendation concerns preserved content, rather than a preference for a filename extension. Reconstructed outputs still require checks appropriate to the planned survival analysis.

The study has several limitations. First, the simulations used exponential or piecewise-exponential event times, one baseline event rate, and one dropout rate. Crossing hazards broadened the design, but other patterns, including Weibull hazards, were not evaluated. Complete risk tables, clean two-arm figures, and limited random censoring before month 24 also provided favorable conditions.

Published figures may contain incomplete risk information, overlapping elements, and different censoring patterns [33] [34] [35]. The number of plotted groups and the complexity of figure legends and labels may also affect reconstruction accuracy. The primary evaluation omitted later follow-up, where administrative censoring accumulated. Second, only one model, reasoning setting, and tool environment were evaluated. Replacement runs and unenforced revision limits mean that the results describe the implemented workflow, rather than first-attempt performance or performance under a uniform revision budget. Third, 16 datasets per scenario and limited repeat runs provide incomplete characterization of scenario-specific and model-run variability. Later exploratory experiments reused earlier baseline outputs, so execution period may also contribute to those contrasts.

Further work should prioritize published-figure validation, comparable reconstruction information and resource limits, and repeated runs under documented model versions. Where original clinical records are unavailable, agreement with reported summaries can assess consistency but cannot establish participant-level truth. Studies with original records can assess downstream estimands directly.

More varied simulations would help identify when reconstruction errors become consequential, rather than merely demonstrating smaller errors in additional favorable examples.

5 Conclusion

Native vector figures supported more accurate reconstruction than matched images in the evaluated language-model workflow, while average differences in treatment estimates remained small. Preserv- Ethics. This study used exclusively simulated data and did not involve human participants.

Therefore, ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
